category_name: Nutrition, swallowing, hydration and mouth care

posts.title: Red plates: what the study was
posts.insight: The advice to use red or high-contrast plates in dementia rests on a 2004 study of nine men and a handful of small, unrandomised studies since. It is cheap to try but not established, and it does not replace help with eating.
posts.angle: Read the red-plate evidence for what it is: small, short, unrandomised, pointing to contrast rather than redness. Try it if you like; do not count it as mealtime support.
posts.position_basis: mixed: study details and review verdict are empirical findings; 'cheap to try' and 'a plate is no substitute for a person' are clinical and ethical judgement

captions.x:
The advice to serve food on red plates in dementia care goes back to a 2004 study of nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease.

Over 10 days with high-contrast red plates and cups, they ate about a quarter more food and drank 84% more on average than over 10 days with white ones. Eight of the nine ate or drank more. No randomisation, no weight outcome.

The same team later found strongly contrasting blue plates also helped; pale red and pale blue did not. That points to contrast, not redness.

A 2026 review found four studies, 64 people in total, none randomised, none longer than a month. It called the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive. A study of blue plates in 18 people did not find a clear increase.

Contrast plates are cheap to try. We should not count a plate in place of a person who helps someone eat.
captions.linkedin:
The advice to serve food on red plates in dementia care goes back to a 2004 study of nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease, living in long-term care.

Over 10 days with high-contrast red plates and cups, they ate about a quarter more food and drank 84% more on average than over 10 days with white ones. Eight of the nine ate or drank more.

Read the design before the headline. The same nine men were studied with white, then red, then white tableware. There was no randomisation. The figures are relative increases in average intake. Nobody measured weight or health.

A year later the same team tried other plates. Strongly contrasting blue plates also increased eating and drinking; pale red and pale blue plates did not. That points to contrast between food and plate, not to the colour red.

A 2026 review searched for every study of contrast at mealtimes. It found four, with 64 people in total; the largest had 25. None was randomised and none lasted more than a month. The reviewers called the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive, and none of the studies showed whether contrast plates prevent weight loss or malnutrition.

The result that went the other way: a later study of blue plates in 18 people with dementia did not find a clear increase in eating. Fewer than a third ate at least a tenth more.

This is an evidence gap, not evidence that contrast does nothing. Most of the studies reported more eating.

My judgement: contrast plates are cheap to try. We should not count a plate in place of a person who sits down and helps someone eat.
captions.bluesky:
Red plates for people with dementia rest on a 2004 study of nine men: about a quarter more food eaten over 10 days, no randomisation, no weight measured.

A 2026 review found 4 small studies, none randomised. Contrast plates are cheap to try. They do not replace help with eating.

posts.title: Mouth care and pneumonia: less certain than the slogan
posts.insight: Trials of extra mouth care in nursing homes have not shown a clear fall in pneumonia; the evidence is uncertain in both directions. Mouth care has firmer reasons to be done well.
posts.angle: Stop selling mouth care as proven pneumonia prevention; describe the pneumonia evidence as uncertain and do mouth care for comfort, eating and dental health.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial and review results are empirical; the reasons to keep doing mouth care are clinical and ethical judgement plus established dental background

captions.x:
Mouth care in nursing homes is often promoted as a way to prevent pneumonia. The trials are less sure.

The largest, in 14 US nursing homes with 2,152 residents, did not show a clear fall over two years: 0.67 against 0.72 pneumonias per 1,000 resident-days. An unplanned look at year one found fewer; in year two there were slightly more.

A 2022 Cochrane review called the effect on pneumonia largely unclear, with a low-certainty signal of fewer pneumonia deaths from two small Japanese trials. Every trial compared extra care with ordinary care, never with none.

So describe the pneumonia benefit as uncertain. We should keep doing mouth care well anyway: it removes plaque, keeps eating comfortable and finds sore spots early.
captions.linkedin:
Mouth care in nursing homes is often promoted as a way to prevent pneumonia. The trials are less sure than that.

The largest trial tested a staff mouth care programme in 14 US nursing homes with 2,152 residents. Over two years it did not show a clear fall in pneumonia: 0.67 cases per 1,000 resident-days against 0.72 without the programme.

Two details keep this from reading as "mouth care does not work". An unplanned analysis of the first year alone found fewer pneumonias. In the second year, pneumonia was slightly (not significantly) more common in programme homes, which the authors linked to difficulty keeping the programme going.

A 2022 Cochrane review pooled six nursing home trials, all at high risk of bias. It concluded that the effect of professional mouth care on pneumonia remains largely unclear. Two small Japanese trials suggested fewer deaths from pneumonia at two years, but that evidence is low certainty, and a larger study found no clear difference at 18 months.

One design point is easy to miss. Every trial compared extra, professional mouth care with ordinary mouth care. None compared mouth care with none. They test how much extra help adds.

So the pneumonia claim should be stated as uncertain in both directions.

My position is that we should keep doing mouth care well whatever the trials show about pneumonia. Cleaning removes plaque, the main cause of tooth decay and gum disease. It keeps eating comfortable. It finds sore spots and broken teeth early.
captions.bluesky:
A trial in 14 US nursing homes (2,152 residents) did not show a clear fall in pneumonia with a mouth care programme. A Cochrane review calls the effect largely unclear.

Say the pneumonia benefit is uncertain. Keep doing mouth care for comfort, eating and teeth.

posts.title: Count the sealed packets on the tray
posts.insight: Many older people struggle to open the portion packs served in hospital, and opening them lying in bed is harder than sitting in a chair. Food that comes back sealed was never available to eat.
posts.angle: Look at the unopened packets on returned trays and treat them as food that was not accessible.
posts.position_basis: mixed: packaging studies are empirical; opening packets, helping people sit up and recording unopened food as not accessible are judgement and advice

captions.x:
Count the sealed packets on a returned hospital tray.

In an Australian study, about 4 in 10 healthy people over 65 could not open a cheese portion, and 1 in 10 could not open a bottle of water. They were well volunteers, not patients.

In four Australian hospitals, about half of 140 mostly older patients found milk, juice and cereal packs difficult to open.

In a laboratory test, opening packs lying in a hospital bed took more finger strength and more nimble fingers than sitting in a chair. The researchers concluded patients should sit up to eat.

UK packs may differ. My advice: open the packets, help the person sit up, and record food that comes back sealed as not reachable, not as refused.
captions.linkedin:
Count the sealed packets on a returned hospital tray.

Food that goes back unopened was never available to eat. Research on hospital packaging suggests this happens more than we assume.

1. In an Australian study, about 4 in 10 healthy people over 65 could not open a hospital cheese portion, and 1 in 10 could not open a bottle of water. They were well volunteers living at home, not patients.

2. In four Australian hospitals, about half of 140 mostly older patients found milk, juice and cereal packs difficult to open.

3. In a laboratory test with 34 healthy older volunteers, opening packs while lying in a hospital bed took more finger strength and more nimble fingers than opening them sitting in a chair. The researchers concluded that patients should sit up to eat.

These studies were done in Australia, mostly with healthy volunteers. Packs in UK hospitals may differ, and I found no UK study. No study here tested whether opening packets increases how much people eat.

My advice, as judgement rather than a trial result. If you work on a ward, open the packets and help the person sit up before you leave the tray. If you are visiting, do the same. And when a tray comes back with sealed packs, record that food as not reachable, not as refused. Those are different problems with different fixes.
captions.bluesky:
About 4 in 10 healthy people over 65 in an Australian study could not open a hospital cheese portion. Opening packs lying in bed took more finger strength than sitting in a chair.

Open the packets. Help the person sit up. Sealed food on the tray was not refused.

posts.title: 38 minutes per meal
posts.insight: Proper one-to-one help with a meal took about 40 minutes per resident in US nursing home studies, against 5 to 9 minutes in usual care. Staffing plans that ignore that time set care workers up to fail.
posts.angle: Count the minutes help with eating takes; plan staffing from that, not from goodwill.
posts.position_basis: mixed: minutes and staffing ratios are empirical; planning staffing from time needed and not blaming care workers is ethical judgement consistent with the authors' conclusion

captions.x:
Helping one nursing home resident through a meal took an average of 38 minutes in a 2001 US study. In usual care, staff gave about 9 minutes.

With that help, half of the 74 residents ate and drank significantly more over two days. The research team gave the help, not the home's staff.

A 2008 US trial found the same pattern: 42 minutes of mostly one-to-one help per meal, against about 5 minutes in usual care. One aide on the day shift looked after 6 to 11 residents.

Care workers are not failing here. We should plan mealtime staffing from the time help takes. No UK figures were found.
captions.linkedin:
Helping one nursing home resident through a meal took an average of 38 minutes in a 2001 US study. In usual care, the home's staff gave about 9 minutes.

During two days of one-to-one help, half of the 74 residents ate and drank significantly more at meals. The other half did not show a significant increase. The help was given by the research team, not the home's own staff.

A later US trial, published in 2008, found the same pattern. Trained research staff took an average of 42 minutes per person to help with a meal, mostly one-to-one. In usual care, residents got about 5 minutes of help per meal.

That trial also reported that 56 in 100 residents kept or gained weight with extra help, against 28 in 100 in usual care. Most of that came from snacks between meals rather than help at meals, so it should not be credited to the mealtime minutes.

Now the staffing. In the homes in that trial, one care aide on the day shift looked after 6 to 11 residents. The researchers wrote that most US nursing homes do not have enough aides to give this help to everyone who needs it.

These are US figures from 2001 and 2008. I found no UK figure.

My judgement: when a resident eats little, the care worker has usually not failed. The plan has. We should plan mealtime staffing from how many people need help and how long the help takes.
captions.bluesky:
In US nursing home studies, helping one resident with a meal took about 40 minutes. Usual care gave 5 to 9. One aide covered 6 to 11 residents.

We should plan mealtime staffing from the time help takes, and stop blaming care workers for the gap.
captions.threads:
Helping one resident with a meal took 38 minutes in a 2001 US nursing home study, and 42 minutes in a 2008 trial. Usual care gave about 9 and about 5 minutes. One aide covered 6 to 11 residents on the day shift.

The researchers said most US homes lack the aides for this help. No UK figure was found.

We should plan staffing from the minutes help takes.

posts.title: Easing a dry mouth in the last days
posts.insight: In the last days of life, frequent mouth and lip care and sips are central to comfort, and families can help. A drip is a separate decision for each person.
posts.angle: Put mouth care first near the end of life; keep assisted hydration as an individual decision, not a default either way.
posts.position_basis: mixed: NICE guidance and study findings are empirical/official; mouth care as a standard and person-by-person drip decisions are clinical judgement

captions.x:
UK guidance on the last days of life asks for frequent care of the mouth and lips, help to drink if the person wants to and can, and support for family who wish to help.

In one small 1994 study of 32 people dying with cancer, thirst and a dry mouth were relieved in every case, usually with mouth care, ice chips, moist lips and sips.

Drips are a separate question. The trials were all in cancer, and a 2023 Cochrane review found too little evidence to say whether they improve comfort. The results do not apply to people dying with dementia.

Mouth care should be standard. The drip should be decided and reviewed for each person.
captions.linkedin:
UK guidance from NICE on the last days of life asks for three things around drinking. Help the person drink if they want to and can. Offer frequent care of the mouth and lips. Encourage family to help with mouth care or drinks if they wish, with advice on doing it safely.

What is the evidence that mouth care eases thirst? It is thin but consistent. In a small US study of 32 people dying with cancer in a comfort care unit, thirst and a dry mouth were relieved in every case, usually by mouth care, ice chips, moistening the lips and sips of drink. The amounts were far smaller than would be needed to prevent dehydration. It was one small study, from 1994, without a comparison group.

Fluids by drip or under the skin are a separate decision. In a trial in six US hospices, 129 people with advanced cancer received either a litre a day or a token 100 mL. The larger amount did not show a clear improvement in symptoms, quality of life or survival. That trial did not measure thirst or dry mouth.

A 2023 Cochrane review found too little evidence to say whether drips improve comfort or prolong life. The trials were all in cancer, and the reviewers say the results do not apply to people dying with dementia or other conditions.

NICE says assisted fluids should be considered and reviewed for each person, for example with distressing thirst, and stopped if they cause harm or are no longer wanted.

My view: frequent mouth care should be a standard part of care in the last days. A drip should be neither given nor withheld by default.
captions.bluesky:
In the last days of life, NICE asks for frequent mouth and lip care, help to drink, and support for family who want to help.

Drip trials were all in cancer, and evidence on comfort is thin. Mouth care should be standard; a drip is decided for each person.
captions.threads:
NICE guidance for the last days of life asks for frequent mouth and lip care, help to drink if wanted, and support for family who want to help.

In one small study of 32 people dying with cancer, mouth care, ice chips and sips relieved thirst in every case.

Evidence on drips is thin and all from cancer. Decide and review a drip for each person.

posts.title: Feeding tubes in severe dementia
posts.insight: Feeding tubes have not been shown to help people with severe dementia live longer or be more comfortable, and one large study linked them with more pressure sores. Careful hand feeding keeps food, drink and company going.
posts.angle: Offer careful hand feeding; do not make tube feeding routine in severe dementia; declining a tube is a decision about one treatment, not about the person.
posts.position_basis: mixed: review findings and guideline positions are empirical/official; the statement about worth is ethical judgement

captions.x:
A feeding tube for a person with severe dementia is a decision about one treatment.

A 2021 Cochrane review found no randomised trials. In 14 observational studies, PEG tubes (a tube into the stomach through the skin) were not shown to help people live longer; low-certainty evidence, and a few small studies pointed the other way. In the largest study, of 4,421 people, pressure sores were slightly more common with a tube. No study showed better comfort.

US and European guidance advise against tubes in severe dementia and recommend careful hand feeding.

Saying no to a tube does not mean stopping care. Food, drink, mouth care and company continue.
captions.linkedin:
A feeding tube for a person with severe dementia is a decision about one treatment.

What does the evidence show? A 2021 Cochrane review found no randomised trials. In 14 observational studies, PEG tubes (a tube into the stomach through the skin) were not shown to help people live longer. The evidence is low certainty, and a few small studies of other tube types pointed the other way. Because none was randomised, people given tubes may have differed in other ways.

In the largest study, of 4,421 people, pressure sores were more common with a PEG tube. The review rated this as moderate certainty and described the increase as small.

No study has shown that a tube makes a person with severe dementia more comfortable. Quality of life was never measured, and the one study that looked at pain and comfort found no difference.

The American Geriatrics Society advises against feeding tubes in advanced dementia and recommends careful hand feeding. European guidance (ESPEN, 2024) says tube feeding can be a temporary option in mild or moderate dementia, but not in severe dementia or near the end of life.

Careful hand feeding is a plan. Offer food regularly. Stop when the person coughs, chokes or shows distress. Write down which foods, times and ways of helping work. Check texture, position, dentures and medicines first. When eating becomes too hard, mouth care, talking and touch continue. It focuses on comfort and will usually not stop weight loss.

My judgement: declining a tube says nothing about a person's worth. We should keep offering food, drink, mouth care and company, guided by what they would have wanted.
captions.bluesky:
Feeding tubes in severe dementia have not been shown to help people live longer or feel more comfortable, and one large study found slightly more pressure sores.

Careful hand feeding is the alternative. Saying no to a tube still means food, drink, mouth care and company.
captions.threads:
A feeding tube in severe dementia is a decision about one treatment.

A Cochrane review found tubes were not shown to help people live longer (low-certainty evidence) or feel more comfortable. One large study found slightly more pressure sores.

US and European guidance favour careful hand feeding. Declining a tube still means food, drink, mouth care and company.

posts.title: Bedside signs are poor tests for dehydration
posts.insight: Single bedside signs such as urine colour, dry mouth and thirst are unreliable for water-loss dehydration in older people; serum osmolality, or a validated calculated osmolarity as a screen, does better.
posts.angle: Stop diagnosing or excluding low-intake dehydration from one bedside sign; use osmolality when the answer changes care.
posts.position_basis: mixed: diagnostic accuracy findings are empirical; 'use osmolality when it changes care' is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Urine colour is a poor test for dehydration in an older person when used on its own. So are dry mouth, thirst, heart rate, urine specific gravity and recorded fluid intake.

A Cochrane review of 24 studies in people 65 and over found each of these, alone, missed many dehydrated people and mislabelled others. This applies to water-loss dehydration from drinking too little.

In 188 UK care home residents, 1 in 5 were dehydrated on a blood test, and thirst was not linked with it.

Use serum osmolality (295 mOsm/kg or more: starting or present). If unavailable, 1.86 x (Na + K) + 1.15 x glucose + urea + 14 at 295 or more caught about 85 in 100 dehydrated people but flagged many who were not. A screen, not a diagnosis.

The Teaching round series takes one bedside shortcut at a time.
captions.linkedin:
Urine colour is a poor test for dehydration in an older person when used on its own.

A Cochrane review pooled 24 studies of people aged 65 and over. Urine colour, urine specific gravity, dry mouth, thirst, heart rate and recorded fluid intake were each not useful alone for spotting or ruling out dehydration. Used alone, they missed many dehydrated people and wrongly labelled others.

Two limits on that finding. It applies to water-loss dehydration from not drinking enough, not to salt-and-water loss from vomiting, diarrhoea or bleeding. And it is about single signs used alone; the observations still have a place in a wider assessment.

The review's reference was serum osmolality: 295 mOsm/kg or more meant dehydration was starting or present, and over 300 meant it was present.

In a UK study of 188 care home residents, average age 86, 1 in 5 were dehydrated on that blood test. Whether residents felt thirsty was not linked with whether they were.

One sign showed promise: missing drinks between meals, in one small study of 71 people. It has not been confirmed elsewhere.

If measured osmolality is not available, estimate it:
1.86 x (Na + K) + 1.15 x glucose + urea + 14, all in mmol/L.
This was the best of 39 formulas tested in 595 older people. At 295 mOsm/L or more it caught about 85 in 100 dehydrated people but also flagged many who were not (specificity 59%). A screen that prompts a closer look, not a diagnosis. Other common formulas performed poorly.

When the answer changes care, send the blood test. The Teaching round series takes one bedside shortcut at a time.
captions.bluesky:
Urine colour, dry mouth and thirst are each unreliable alone for spotting low-intake dehydration in older people (Cochrane, 24 studies).

In 188 UK care home residents, 1 in 5 were dehydrated on a blood test; thirst was not linked. Use serum osmolality.

posts.title: When food tastes of nothing
posts.insight: Many older people have lost much of their sense of smell without knowing it, and smell is a large part of flavour. Stronger flavours are worth trying, and a recently started medicine can be worth asking about.
posts.angle: Ask whether food still smells of anything; try stronger flavours, and check medicines with the GP or pharmacist.
posts.position_basis: mixed: smell loss prevalence and trial results are empirical; the suggestions are practical advice

captions.x:
Does food still smell of anything to you?

In a US study of 2,491 people aged 53 to 97, about 6 in 10 of those aged 80 and over had a weakened sense of smell when tested. Most did not know.

Smell is one of the biggest parts of flavour. A weaker sense of smell can make food seem to taste of less. Illness, medicines, smoking and a blocked nose can add to it.

Stronger flavours are worth trying: sauces, herbs, a squeeze of lemon. The evidence is mixed. One Dutch care home study found weight gain with flavour-enhanced meals; a later trial found no change.

If food has tasted wrong since a new medicine, ask your GP or pharmacist. Do not stop it on your own.
captions.linkedin:
Does food still smell of anything to you?

It is a fair question to ask an older relative whose appetite has faded. In a US population study of 2,491 people aged 53 to 97, about 1 in 4 had a weakened sense of smell when tested. Among those aged 80 and over it was about 6 in 10. Most people with a weak sense of smell did not know they had it.

Smell is one of the biggest parts of the flavour of food. A weaker sense of smell can make food less enjoyable and seem to taste of less. Smell and taste can fade with age, but illness, medicines, smoking and a blocked nose can also cause or worsen it. Taste loss, mouth problems and low mood can play a part too.

What can you try?

1. Stronger flavours: sauces, herbs, pepper, a squeeze of lemon. These are reasonable suggestions, but they have not been tested in trials.

2. Know that the evidence on adding flavour is mixed. In one Dutch care home study, residents given flavour-enhanced meals gained about 1 kg over 16 weeks while others lost a little. A later randomised trial by the same group found no change in how much residents ate or weighed. Both used commercial flavour enhancers.

3. Ask about medicines. Many medicines can dull or change taste, including some blood pressure tablets, antibiotics and antidepressants. How often this happens is not well known.

If food has tasted wrong since a medicine was started, ask your GP or pharmacist. Do not stop a medicine on your own.
captions.bluesky:

posts.title: Take the dentures out at night
posts.insight: Dental specialists advise taking dentures out every night and cleaning them daily. In a study of people aged 85 and over, sleeping in dentures was linked with more serious pneumonia, though the link does not prove cause.
posts.angle: Take dentures out at night and clean them daily; treat the pneumonia link as an association.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the study association and expert advice are empirical/expert; the instruction is practical advice

captions.x:
In a Japanese study of 524 people aged 85 and over, about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept with their dentures in.

Over three years, they were more likely to be admitted to hospital with pneumonia, or to die of it, than people who took them out, even after allowing for other measured health differences. This link does not show that dentures at night cause pneumonia.

They also had more plaque, more gum inflammation and more thrush-type yeast in the mouth.

Dental specialists advise taking dentures out every night and cleaning them every day, mainly to prevent sore gums. Follow your own dentist's advice if it differs.
captions.linkedin:
In a Japanese study of 524 people aged 85 and over living at home, about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept with their dentures in.

Over three years, those who slept in their dentures were more likely to be admitted to hospital with pneumonia, or to die of it, than those who took them out. This held after the researchers allowed for other health differences they measured.

Read that result carefully. It is a link, not proof. People who sleep in dentures may differ in health, frailty or the help they get, in ways the study did not measure. There were only 48 pneumonia events, so the size of the link is uncertain. And the outcome was pneumonia serious enough for hospital admission or death.

At the start of the study, people who slept in their dentures also had more plaque on the tongue and dentures, more gum inflammation, and more thrush-type yeast (Candida) in the mouth.

What should you do? Dental specialists advise taking dentures out at night, every night, and cleaning them every day. Their main reason is to prevent sore, inflamed gums under the denture. That advice stands whatever the pneumonia link turns out to mean.

If you help a parent or partner with their dentures, taking them out at bedtime and cleaning them is a small nightly task with a clear reason behind it.

If your own dentist has told you something different, follow their advice.

Dental specialists advise taking dentures out every night and cleaning them daily, mainly to prevent sore gums.

posts.title: When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away
posts.insight: A set of calm techniques helped mouth care get done more often for people with dementia who resisted it, though refusals continued. The aim is getting mouth care done, not ending every refusal.
posts.angle: Change the approach before deciding brushing is impossible.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial results are empirical; the fear idea is the authors' theory; 'change the approach first' is practical judgement

captions.x:
When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away, the approach can change before anyone gives up.

In a US trial in nine nursing homes, 101 people with dementia who often refused mouth care were split at random. With a set of calm techniques, mouth care was accepted and finished more often, and lasted longer.

The techniques: come at or below eye level; brush at a sink in front of a mirror; hand them the brush; start and let them carry on; one-step instructions; gently guide the hand; swap carer if it escalates.

Refusals did not stop, and mouth health showed no clear difference over three weeks. Research staff gave the care.
captions.linkedin:
When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away, the approach can change before anyone decides brushing is not possible.

The idea behind one approach is that pushing a toothbrush away is often fear. Having someone put something in your mouth can feel like a threat if you are unable to follow what is happening.

A US trial in nine nursing homes tested this. 101 people with dementia who often refused mouth care were split at random into two groups. When carers used a set of calm techniques, mouth care was accepted and finished more often, and lasted longer, than with carers who cleaned teeth well without those techniques.

The techniques included:

1. Coming to the person calmly, at or below eye level.
2. Doing mouth care at a sink, in front of a mirror.
3. Giving the person a toothbrush to hold.
4. Starting the brushing and letting them carry on.
5. Gestures and short, one-step instructions.
6. Gently guiding their hand.
7. If things escalate, letting a different carer take over.

Carers tried different techniques to find what worked for each person. The trial tested the whole set, not each one separately.

The limits are real. Refusals did not stop. Over three weeks the trial did not show a clear difference in mouth health or in resistance. Trained research staff gave the care, and people with swallowing problems were excluded.

The researchers concluded that the aim is to get mouth care done despite some refusal, not to make refusal disappear. That is a useful aim for any family or care team.
captions.bluesky:
When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away, try another approach: eye level, a mirror, a brush in their hand.

In a US trial, calm techniques like these got mouth care done more often. Refusals did not stop.
captions.threads:
When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away, change the approach first.

In a US trial with 101 nursing home residents, calm techniques got mouth care accepted and finished more often: come at eye level, use a sink and mirror, hand them the brush, let them carry on, swap carer if needed.

posts.title: Family style meals in nursing homes
posts.insight: In a Dutch trial, residents without dementia whose wards switched to family style meals held their weight and quality of life steady, while those on plated meals lost ground.
posts.angle: Family style mealtimes, with staff sitting at the table, are worth offering to residents able to take part; the benefit is shown in people without dementia.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial results are empirical; offering it is clinical judgement

captions.x:
Tablecloths, proper plates, dishes on the table and a member of staff sitting down to chat at every table.

A Dutch trial randomly gave some nursing home wards these family style meals for six months, and others the usual plated meals. The 178 residents did not have dementia.

With family style meals, weight and quality of life held steady and residents ate more. With plated meals, residents lost about 1 kg and quality of life fell.

The trial tested the whole package, not self-service alone. In dementia, a review calls it promising but not yet shown in trials. Nursing homes, not hospitals.
captions.linkedin:
Tablecloths, proper plates, dishes on the table and a member of staff sitting down to chat at every table.

That was the change tested in a Dutch trial in five nursing homes. Wards were randomly assigned to family style meals or the usual plated meals for six months. The 178 residents did not have dementia; many had conditions such as stroke or Parkinson's disease.

Family style meant more than shared dishes. Tables had cloths, glasses and proper plates. Food came in dishes and most residents served themselves. A member of staff sat and chatted at every table, and nothing else happened in the dining room during the meal.

Over six months, residents who ate family style held their weight steady, while those given plated meals lost about 1 kg; the gap between groups was 1.5 kg. Quality of life held steady with family style meals and fell with plated meals. Residents eating family style also ate more.

Two things to read carefully. The advantage is mostly that the plated group got worse. And the trial tested the whole package, so it does not tell us which part helped.

For people with dementia, a review lists family style meals as promising, but the studies are small and short.

This was in nursing homes; hospital wards were not studied.

My view: for residents who can take part, a shared table with staff sitting at it is a good model of care, and one worth offering.

In dementia it is promising but not yet shown in trials.
